When fire, a bell or horn were proposed to signal prayer, Umar suggested a man calling, and Bilal was ordered to say the adhan's words twice and the iqama's once.
Satan flees from the adhan and iqama, then returns to distract worshippers; all who hear the caller witness for him, and the Prophet held off attacking where adhan was heard.
Hearers repeat the caller's words, and the invocation after it earns the Prophet's intercession; knowing the reward, people would draw lots for the adhan and first row.
In rain the caller said pray at home; Bilal's adhan came at night so eating continued until Ibn Umm Maktum's at dawn, and two light rak'at preceded Fajr's iqama.
Men going home and travellers were told to call the adhan and iqama and let the eldest lead; on a journey the Prophet delayed the Zuhr adhan until it cooled.
One of a group calls the Adhan and the eldest leads; on cold or rainy nights the caller adds 'Pray at your homes'; Bilal turned his face while calling.
Bilal's adhan comes while it is still night, so eat and drink until the blind Ibn Um Maktum's adhan at dawn.
Leaving the Prophet, Malik bin al-Huwairith and a friend are told to give the adhan and iqama themselves and let the elder lead the prayer.
Raise your voice in the adhan, Abu Sa'id tells a man fond of sheep and desert, for every human, jinn or thing hearing it will testify for him.
Bilal's adhan at night does not stop suhur, for it lets night worshippers return to eat and sleepers wake; eat and drink until Ibn Um Maktum's adhan.
Abu Sa'id told a shepherd to raise his voice in the adhan, for every jinn, human or thing that hears the caller will witness for him on Resurrection.
